# Evaluating LLM Systems {#sec-llm-eval}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** The judge audit runs `qwen3.5:9b` and
`gemma3:27b` through `ollama` 0.24.0 on 60 XL-Sum Turkish articles; the
sizing tables are simulated with `scipy` and checked against the closed-form
result. Software: NumPy 2.5.2, `scipy` 1.18.1, `ollama` 0.24.0 on Python
3.14.5.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- distinguish model benchmarks from *system* evaluation, and know which one
  you need;
- size an eval set from the difference you need to detect, rather than from
  what felt reasonable;
- audit an LLM judge before believing it, with controls that have known
  right answers;
- report results with uncertainty, and choose a paired design when it
  actually helps.

This is the chapter your statistics training was made for: applied LLM
evaluation is, at bottom, [measurement design under distribution
shift]{.hl}. Most of what follows is not new statistics. It is ordinary
statistics applied to a setting where almost nobody applies it.

## Benchmarks are not your evaluation {#sec-llm-eval-benchmarks}

A public benchmark answers *how does this model compare to other models on a
task someone else chose*. Your evaluation answers *does this system do my job
well enough to ship*. Those are different questions and the first one is only
occasionally evidence about the second.

Three specific reasons, in the order they will bite you.

**[Contamination](#gloss-benchmark-contamination){#term-benchmark-contamination .term-ref}.**
A benchmark published before a model was trained may be inside that model's
training data, and you usually cannot check.

::: {#gloss-benchmark-contamination .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Benchmark contamination** — test items that were in a model's training data,
so its score reports memorisation rather than capability. Usually
unmeasurable from outside, which is why it is a reason to distrust benchmarks
rather than a thing to correct for.
[↩](#term-benchmark-contamination){.term-back}
:::

This book
measured the effect on a smaller scale in @sec-sequence-labeling: **13.06% of
WikiANN's Turkish test set is byte-identical to a training sentence**, and the
score bonus that leakage produced fell monotonically with how much a system
memorises — +26.50 span F1 for a gazetteer, +16.25 for a CRF, +7.65 for a
fine-tuned encoder. Nobody had to be dishonest for that to happen.

**Saturation.** When the headline models are at 88, 89 and 90, the benchmark
has stopped measuring capability and started measuring the last few percent of
label noise. Differences at the top of a saturated leaderboard are frequently
smaller than that benchmark's own error rate.

**Construct mismatch.** The benchmark measures a task; you have a *system*,
which is a prompt, a retrieval step, a parser, a fallback, and a model. A
benchmark score cannot tell you that your JSON parser drops 2% of responses —
@sec-decoding measured a case where formatting failures were being counted as
reasoning failures, and enforcement moved accuracy from 70.7% to 88.0% with no
change to the model at all.

::: {.column-margin}
The useful role for public benchmarks is *screening*: they cheaply eliminate
models that are obviously unfit, and they tell you what is broadly possible.
Treat a leaderboard as a way to pick three candidates, never as a way to pick
one.
:::

## How big does your eval set need to be? {#sec-llm-eval-size}

Here is the question almost every LLM project answers by feel, and it has an
exact answer. Given a system that is right about 80% of the time, how large
must an eval set be to detect an improvement of *d* points, at 80%
[**statistical power**](#gloss-statistical-power){#term-statistical-power .term-ref}
and the conventional 5% significance level?

::: {#gloss-statistical-power .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Statistical power** — the probability that your evaluation detects a real
difference of a given size. Low power does not produce wrong answers; it
produces *no* answer, reported as if it were one.
[↩](#term-statistical-power){.term-back}
:::

```text
smallest difference detectable at 80% power (two proportions, base 80%)

     items      smallest detectable difference
        30            none — see below
        50                    17.5 points
       100                    13.4 points
       200                    10.0 points
       500                     6.6 points
     1,000                     4.8 points
     2,000                     3.4 points
```

::: {.anlp-widget}
```{=html}
<div class="widget-title">Size your own eval set</div>
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof evalBase = Inputs.range([0.50, 0.95], {step: 0.01, value: 0.80,
  label: "current accuracy"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof evalDiff = Inputs.range([1, 20], {step: 1, value: 5,
  label: "difference you need to detect (points)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof evalPower = Inputs.radio(new Map([["80%", 0.80], ["90%", 0.90]]),
  {value: 0.80, label: "power"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Abramowitz–Stegun 26.2.23 inverse normal, good to ~4.5e-4 — plenty here
evalZ = p => {
  const t = Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(p < 0.5 ? p : 1 - p));
  const x = t - (2.515517 + 0.802853 * t + 0.010328 * t * t) /
            (1 + 1.432788 * t + 0.189269 * t * t + 0.001308 * t * t * t);
  return p < 0.5 ? -x : x;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
evalN = {
  const d = evalDiff / 100, pa = evalBase, pb = Math.min(pa + d, 0.999);
  const za = evalZ(0.975), zb = evalZ(evalPower);
  const pbar = (pa + pb) / 2;
  const n = Math.pow(za * Math.sqrt(2 * pbar * (1 - pbar)) +
                     zb * Math.sqrt(pa * (1 - pa) + pb * (1 - pb)), 2) / (d * d);
  return Math.ceil(n);
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`To detect **${evalDiff} points** on top of ${(evalBase * 100).toFixed(0)}%
at ${(evalPower * 100).toFixed(0)}% power, you need about
**${evalN.toLocaleString()} items per system** — ${evalN > 500
  ? "more than most teams label, which is the useful thing to find out before running the comparison rather than after"
  : "a size you can realistically label"}.
A paired design needs fewer *if* the two systems mostly agree, and fewer still
the more they agree; see the table below.`
```
:::

[At thirty items there is no answer, because no difference is large enough.]{.hl}
Against a system that is right 80% of the time, even a *perfect* replacement —
one that is right 100% of the time — reaches only 75% power on thirty items.
A hundred items detects 13.4 points. Most real improvements are two to five.

That is worth sitting with, because thirty items is a common size; it is the
size this chapter's own exercise asked for in draft.

This does **not** mean small eval sets are useless. It means they answer a
different question, and the distinction is the most practically useful thing
in this chapter:

| eval set size | what it is genuinely for |
|:--|:--|
| **20–50 items** | finding *failure modes*. Read every output by hand. You are looking for categories of wrongness, not for a number, and thirty items surfaces them well — this is a real job, and the size is right for it |
| **100–300 items** | catching *large* regressions — a broken parser, a prompt that stopped working, a model swap that went badly |
| **500+ items** | comparing two systems that are actually close, which is the case whenever you are tuning rather than fixing |

: Three different jobs, three different sizes {tbl-colwidths="[22,78]"}

The failure to distinguish these is why so much prompt engineering is
folklore. Thirty examples were tried, one prompt looked better, and the
difference was smaller than the noise floor by an order of magnitude.

### What pairing buys, and when it does not

@sec-prompting used McNemar's test to establish a 14.67-point spread that
overlapping confidence intervals would have called inconclusive. The
comparison there was **paired** — the same 150 reviews through every prompt —
and pairing is the standard advice.

The advice is right and it is not unconditional, because McNemar's test throws
away every item the two systems agree on. So what pairing buys depends on how
often they disagree, which is an empirical property of *your* systems:

```text
power to detect a 5-point difference (alpha = 0.05)

   items   unpaired    paired, by how often the two systems disagree
                          10%       20%       30%       40%
      30       0.08      0.01      0.03      0.03      0.04
      50       0.10      0.07      0.06      0.07      0.05
     100       0.15      0.24      0.14      0.10      0.10
     200       0.26      0.55      0.30      0.21      0.16
     500       0.56      0.94      0.68      0.51      0.39
   1,000       0.84      1.00      0.94      0.81      0.69
```

**Pairing pays when your systems mostly agree.** At 10% disagreement it more
than doubles your power at n = 200. At 30% it is a wash. At 40% it is worse
than the unpaired test, because there are so many discordant pairs that the
test is estimating a coin flip from a large sample rather than exploiting
agreement.

That has a clean practical reading. Comparing two prompts, two checkpoints, or
two decoding settings — cases where the systems agree on most items — use the
paired design and gain real power. Comparing two genuinely different
architectures that disagree constantly, pairing buys you little, and the honest
move is a bigger eval set rather than a cleverer test.

::: {.column-margin}
I got this backwards on the first attempt. I fixed the disagreement rate at
@sec-prompting's measured 30.7%, found that pairing was *worse* than the
unpaired test, and briefly believed I had refuted a textbook result. The
simulation was right; the framing was wrong — a single disagreement rate
cannot answer a question whose whole content is how the answer varies with
that rate. The closed-form check in the script would not have caught it either,
because the unpaired side was correct all along.
:::

## Building an eval set {#sec-llm-eval-building}

An eval set is a **sample**, and everything your statistics training says
about samples applies. Three decisions do almost all the work.

**Sample from real traffic, not from imagination.** Invented test cases are
systematically cleaner, better spelled, and more typical than what users send.
If you have no traffic yet, use whatever is closest — support tickets, search
logs, a colleague's real questions — and label the gap explicitly. A hundred
real items beat a thousand invented ones, and this is the single highest-value
decision in the chapter.

**Stratify deliberately, then say what you did.** Real traffic is dominated by
easy cases, so a uniform sample spends most of its items confirming that the
easy cases still work. Oversample the hard slices, the rare-but-costly
categories, and the languages you actually serve — and then, when you report a
headline number, either reweight to the traffic distribution or say plainly
that the number is on a stratified sample. Both are fine; silence is not.

**Include the cases with no good answer.** Questions your system should refuse,
inputs that are out of scope, documents that do not contain the answer.
@sec-rag found this to be the test nobody runs, and @sec-multimodal found a
model that refused 90 times out of 90 when asked for something absent — a
result you only learn by asking.

### Label the data before you look at model output

The order matters more than it sounds. Labels written after seeing a system's
answers drift toward those answers, and the drift is invisible afterwards.
Write the rubric, label a sample against it, measure how often two labellers
agree, and *then* run anything. If agreement between two humans is 70%, no
system can score meaningfully above 70% and every point above that is noise
you are reading as signal — @sec-data-annotation has the machinery.

### Version the eval like code

The eval set is a dependency of every number you report, so it belongs in the
repository, in a file, under review, with a changelog. Two rules that pay for
themselves:

- **Never edit an item in place.** Add a new one and retire the old, so a
  score from March remains comparable to a score from June, and a score that
  moved because the *test* changed is distinguishable from one that moved
  because the system did.
- **Keep a held-out slice you look at rarely.** An eval set you tune against
  every day is a training set. @sec-classification's split discipline is the
  same discipline, one level up.

### The harness bugs that produce good numbers

A broken evaluation harness usually does not crash. It reports something
plausible, and there is an asymmetry that makes this dangerous: **a bad number
gets investigated, a good one gets published.** Two bugs from this book's own
work, both caught late:

- A reasoning model was given a 24-token generation budget. `ollama` returns
  chain-of-thought in a separate `thinking` field, so the whole budget went
  there, the answer field stayed empty, every response failed to parse, and
  each failure fell through to a majority-class default. The run reported
  **93.75% accuracy** — which was exactly the majority baseline.
- A tuned threshold was applied to the wrong side of a probability, scoring a
  model at 51.50 macro-F1 instead of 80.23.

Neither raised an error. The guards that would have caught them are cheap:
**log the parse rate per run and abort below 50%**, smoke-test every
model×condition on two dozen items before an overnight queue, and quote
*median* seconds per item rather than the mean — machine stalls in this book's
own runs made one mean nine times its median.

## LLM-as-judge, audited {#sec-llm-eval-judge}

Using a model to grade another model's output is now the default for anything
that cannot be scored with an exact match. It is a reasonable idea and it is
also **a measuring instrument you did not calibrate**. So calibrate it — with
probes whose right answer you already know, which means you can score the
judge rather than trust it.

Three probes, on 60 Turkish news articles, comparing summaries:

1. **Identical.** A and B are the same text. The only correct verdict is a
   tie. This is @sec-summarization's copied-text control, moved from metrics
   to preferences.
2. **Position.** A real comparison — the professional summary against the
   article's first sentence — run in **both orders**. A judge without
   [**position bias**](#gloss-position-bias){#term-position-bias .term-ref}
   returns the same winner both times.

3. **Verbosity.** The same summary, padded with contentless filler. No
   information is added, so preferring the padded version is preferring
   length.

::: {#gloss-position-bias .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Position bias** — a judge preferring whichever candidate it saw first.
Measured directly by running the same comparison in both orders and counting
how often the verdict flips. [↩](#term-position-bias){.term-back}
:::

```text
                                       qwen3.5:9b     gemma3:27b     Fisher p

 1. identical texts → called a tie        100.0%         100.0%            —

 2. same winner in both orders             61.7%          85.0%      0.00674
    picked whichever was in slot A         57.5%          54.2%            —
    preferred the professional summary     51.7%          74.2%      0.00048

 3. preferred the padded copy              28.3%           0.0%      <0.0001
```

### Both judges pass the test everyone runs

The identical-text control is the sanity check a careful team would think to
run, and **both models score 100%**. Sixty pairs of byte-identical text, sixty
ties, no exceptions. If that were your whole audit you would conclude you have
two sound judges and pick on price.

Then the probes that discriminate:

[The small judge changes its answer on 38% of items when you swap the
order.]{.hl} Same two texts, same question, different verdict. That is not a
hard-comparison problem — it is a property of the instrument, and it means
more than a third of its verdicts carry no information about the summaries at
all.

It is also **at chance** on the actual comparison: 51.7% for the professional
BBC summary over the article's opening sentence, with a confidence interval
[42.8, 60.4] that comfortably contains 50. In fairness to the model, a news
lead is a genuinely strong summary — @sec-summarization measured lead-3 at
14.03 ROUGE-1 against an extractive oracle of 24.89, so this is not an absurd
thing to find difficult. But a judge that cannot separate those two should not
be ranking your system's outputs either.

The larger judge is better on every probe: 85.0% order-consistency, 74.2% on
the real comparison, and it never once fell for the padding. All three
differences are significant at n = 60.

::: {.column-margin}
Which is a nice internal check on @sec-llm-eval-size: the sizing table says an
eval of 50 items detects a 17.5-point difference, and the judge gap here is
23.3 points at n = 60. The experiment was adequately powered *for the
difference it found* — and would have been badly underpowered for a 5-point
one, which is worth remembering before reading anything into the slot-A
numbers (57.5% against 54.2%), where the design has no power at all.
:::

### Verbosity bias did not reproduce

The folklore says judges prefer longer answers. Neither of these did:
`qwen3.5:9b` preferred the padded copy 28.3% of the time and `gemma3:27b`
never. I will state that narrowly, the way @sec-rag's needle result had to be
stated: my filler was **obviously** contentless boilerplate — three sentences
of "the situation is as described above" — and detecting that is a much easier
task than resisting a genuinely more detailed, better-organised, longer answer.
What I measured is that both judges reject obvious padding. What I did not
measure is what they do with elaboration that adds real structure but no
correctness, which is the case the folklore is actually about.

### What to do about it

- **Run the probes before you run the eval.** All three take an afternoon and
  they change which judge you use.
- **Randomise or average over order.** Present each pair in both orders and
  count only the items where the verdict agrees, or randomise and accept the
  extra variance. Reporting a single-order pairwise result from a judge with
  38% flip rate is reporting the coin, not the systems.
- **Prefer pairwise over absolute scoring**, but know what it costs. Asking
  "which is better" is more reliable than asking for a 1–5 rating, because a
  rating scale drifts between calls and has no anchor. The cost is that
  pairwise comparisons do not aggregate into a score without more structure.
- **Calibrate against human labels on a subsample.** Fifty items labelled by
  hand tells you the judge's agreement rate with the thing you actually care
  about. Without that number, a judge score is a measurement in unknown units.
- **Never let the judge be the same model as the system under test**, or at
  least never without measuring the self-preference that setup invites.

## Reporting a result someone can act on {#sec-llm-eval-reporting}

A number without an interval is a rumour. Four rules, all cheap:

**Report an interval, and say how you got it.** For a proportion, Wilson
beats the textbook normal approximation at the small sample sizes this field
actually uses — it does not produce impossible bounds below 0 or above 1.
Every percentage in this chapter carries one.

**Use the paired test when the systems mostly agree**, per
@sec-llm-eval-size, and say which you used. Two overlapping marginal intervals
are not evidence of no difference: @sec-prompting's 14.67-point spread had
overlapping intervals and McNemar found p = 0.0009.

**Quote medians for latency, never means.** One stalled request rewrites a
mean. This book's own timing runs produced a mean nine times its median, and a
concurrent job made one configuration look nineteen times slower than an
identical one — which is why no chapter here publishes a latency number
collected while something else was running.

**Report coverage alongside accuracy whenever anything can abstain, fail to
parse, or time out.** An accuracy computed only over successful responses is
not an accuracy — @sec-decoding's abstention result moved 86.75% to 92.50%
purely by declining the hardest fifth, which is an improvement only if you
also say you answered 80% of the questions.

### Regression testing, which is the point of all this

The eval set earns its keep when a change lands. Run it on every prompt
change, model version, and dependency bump, and store the per-item results
rather than the summary — because the useful question after a drop is *which
items changed*, and a stored aggregate cannot answer it.

Two thresholds worth agreeing in advance, before anyone has a stake in the
answer: the size of drop that blocks a release, and the size that merely opens
an investigation. Set them from @sec-llm-eval-size's table rather than from a
round number, because a rule that blocks on a 2-point drop in a 100-item eval
will fire constantly on noise and then be ignored, which is worse than having
no rule.

## Lab: audit a judge, then size your eval {#sec-llm-eval-lab}

### Step 1 — write 50 items from real traffic

Real inputs, and include five your system should refuse. Label them yourself
before running anything.

### Step 2 — measure human agreement

Have a second person label 25 of them. Compute agreement. That number is the
ceiling on every score you will report afterwards.

### Step 3 — run the identical-text probe

Ask your judge to compare an output with itself, 30 times. If it does not call
a tie, stop and fix the prompt before doing anything else.

### Step 4 — run the position probe

Take 30 real comparisons and run each in both orders. Report the flip rate. If
it is above about 20%, every single-order result you have collected so far is
partly noise.

### Step 5 — calibrate against your own labels

On the 50 labelled items, how often does the judge agree with you? That is the
number that converts judge scores into something meaningful.

### Step 6 — size the next eval

Decide the smallest difference that would change a decision. Use
@sec-llm-eval-size's table to find the item count it requires. If the count is
larger than you can label, say so explicitly rather than shipping an
underpowered comparison and calling it a result.

### What to hand in

The two probe results, the judge–human agreement rate, the human–human
agreement rate, and one sentence naming the smallest difference your eval set
can actually detect.

## Intuition checks {#sec-llm-eval-intuition}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Your model scores 91 on a public benchmark. What have you learned?

That it is not obviously unfit, and little else. You have not learned whether
the benchmark was in its training data — @sec-sequence-labeling found **13.06%
of one benchmark's test set duplicated in its own training split** — nor
whether the benchmark is saturated, nor whether it measures your task.
Benchmarks are a screen for picking three candidates. Your eval decides
between them.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Is a 30-item eval set worth building?

Yes, for the right question — but not for comparing systems. At thirty items
there is **no** difference detectable at 80% power against an 80%-accurate
baseline: even a replacement that is right every single time reaches only 75%.
What thirty items is excellent at is *finding failure modes*: read all thirty outputs by hand and
you will find categories of wrongness that no aggregate score would surface.
Use small sets to learn what breaks, large sets to decide what ships.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Should you always use a paired test?

Usually, but know why. McNemar discards every item the systems agree on, so
its power depends on the disagreement rate. Measured here: at 10% disagreement
pairing more than doubles power at n = 200; at 30% it is a wash; at **40% it
is worse** than the unpaired test. Comparing two prompts — which agree on most
items — pair. Comparing two very different systems, pairing buys little and a
bigger eval set is the honest fix.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Your LLM judge gives two identical texts a tie every time. Is it reliable?

You have learned that it passes the easiest possible check, and nothing more.
Both judges here scored **100%** on that probe and then diverged sharply: one
flipped its verdict on 38% of items when the order was swapped and was at
chance on the real comparison; the other flipped on 15% and was at 74.2%. The
control everyone runs is the one that discriminates least.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. Two prompts score 84% and 79% on your 100-item eval. Is the first better?

You cannot tell from those numbers. A 100-item eval detects about **13 points**
at 80% power, and this is 5. If the comparison is paired — the same 100 items
through both prompts — run McNemar on the disagreements, which may well find
it. If it is not paired, the honest report is "no detectable difference at this
sample size", which is a different statement from "no difference".
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. Your eval harness reports 93.75% accuracy. What do you check first?

The parse rate. That exact number came from a run where a reasoning model
spent its whole token budget in a `thinking` field, every answer failed to
parse, and each failure defaulted to the majority class — so the harness was
reporting the **majority baseline** as a result. A bad number gets
investigated and a good one gets published, so a suspiciously good number
deserves the same scrutiny a bad one gets automatically.
:::

## Exercises {#sec-llm-eval-exercises}

1. **Size your current eval.** Take an eval set you already use, find its item
   count in @sec-llm-eval-size's table, and write down the smallest difference
   it can detect. Compare that to the differences you have been reporting.
2. **Audit your judge.** Run the identical-text and position probes on
   whatever judge you use now. Report the tie rate and the flip rate.
3. **Both orders.** Take a pairwise evaluation you have already run and rerun
   it with the order swapped. How many verdicts change? What does that do to
   your conclusion?
4. **Find the agreement ceiling.** Have two people label the same 30 items
   independently. Compute agreement. Compare it to the accuracy you have been
   reporting for your system.
5. **Build the absence slice.** Add ten items your system should refuse.
   Measure how often it does. This is usually the fastest way to find a real
   problem.
6. **Break your own harness.** Set a generation budget too small for a
   reasoning model and see what your pipeline reports. Then add the parse-rate
   guard that would have caught it.
7. **Power in reverse.** Pick the smallest improvement that would change a
   decision at your organisation. Compute the eval size it needs. If you
   cannot afford it, write down what you will do instead — that sentence is a
   more useful deliverable than most eval reports.

## Interview questions {#sec-llm-eval-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.**
:::

### Testing whether you understand the measurement

**Q: How would you evaluate an LLM feature?**

Start by separating the two questions — is the model capable, and does my
system work — and say that public benchmarks answer only the first. Then give
the structure: a versioned eval set sampled from real traffic, sized from the
difference you need to detect, including cases the system should refuse, with
human labels collected before any model output is seen. Finish on reporting:
intervals, paired tests where the systems mostly agree, and coverage alongside
accuracy.

**Q: Your eval set has 100 items and the new prompt scores 5 points higher.
Ship it?**

Not on that evidence. A hundred items detects about 13 points at 80% power, so
5 points is inside the noise — unless the design is paired, in which case run
McNemar on the disagreements, which can find effects the marginal intervals
cannot. The answer that shows judgement is naming what you would do next:
either enlarge the eval, or ship it as a low-risk change while explicitly not
claiming an improvement.

**Q: What is wrong with using GPT-4-class models as judges?**

Nothing, provided you calibrate one first. The failure is treating it as an
oracle rather than an instrument. Name the specific biases and how you would
measure each: position, by running both orders — measured here at a 38% flip
rate for a small judge and 15% for a large one; verbosity, by padding an
answer without adding information; self-preference, by never letting the judge
grade its own family without checking. And calibrate against human labels on a
subsample, because otherwise the score has no units.

### Testing whether you have shipped one

**Q: How do you catch a broken evaluation?**

With controls that have known answers, because a broken harness usually
returns something plausible rather than crashing. Score a reference against
itself and require a perfect result. Log the parse rate and abort below a
threshold. Compare against a majority-class baseline every run — if your model
matches it exactly, that is a bug and not a coincidence. And say the thing
that makes all of it necessary: a bad number gets investigated, a good one
gets published.

**Q: Your production quality dropped and the eval did not move. What
happened?**

Most likely the eval no longer resembles traffic — inputs drifted, a new
customer segment arrived, or the eval was built from imagined cases in the
first place. Check the input distribution before touching the model. The
second candidate is that the failure is in a part of the system the eval does
not exercise: a parser, a retrieval step, a timeout. That is why per-item
results are stored rather than aggregates, and why coverage is reported
alongside accuracy.


## Where to go deeper {#sec-llm-eval-deeper}

Before reading anything: count the items in your current eval set and look up
the smallest difference it can detect. If you have been reporting differences
below that, everything else here is urgent.

| resource | what it is |
|:--|:--|

## What to remember {#sec-llm-eval-summary}

- **A public benchmark screens; your eval decides.** Contamination is real and
  usually unmeasurable from outside — @sec-sequence-labeling found **13.06%**
  of one benchmark's test set duplicated in its training split — and a
  saturated leaderboard measures label noise rather than capability.
- **Size the eval from the difference you need to detect.** At 80% power on a
  system that is right 80% of the time, **30 items can detect nothing at all**
  — even a perfect replacement reaches only 75% power — 100 items detects 13.4
  points, and 1,000 detects 4.8. Most real improvements are 2–5 points, so most
  eval sets in use cannot see the thing they were built to see.
- **Small eval sets are for finding failure modes, not for comparing
  systems.** Twenty to fifty items read by hand will tell you *what* breaks.
  Five hundred or more is what it takes to tell you *which is better*.
- **Pairing helps in proportion to how much the systems agree.** At 10%
  disagreement it more than doubles power; at 30% it is a wash; at **40% it is
  worse** than the unpaired test, because McNemar discards every agreement.
- **Audit the judge with controls that have known answers.** Both judges here
  scored **100%** on identical-text ties — and then one flipped its verdict on
  **38% of items** when the order was swapped and sat at chance (51.7%) on the
  real comparison, while the other flipped on 15% and reached 74.2%. The
  control everyone runs is the one that discriminates least.
- **Run pairwise comparisons in both orders**, and count only the items where
  the two agree. A single-order result from a judge with a 38% flip rate is
  reporting the coin.
- **Verbosity bias did not reproduce here** — neither judge preferred an
  obviously padded copy — but that is a narrow claim about obvious padding,
  not about the elaborate-but-empty answers the folklore is really about.
- **A bad number gets investigated; a good one gets published.** That
  asymmetry, not the bug, is what to design against. Log parse rates, keep a
  majority-class baseline in every run, score a reference against itself, and
  treat a suspiciously good result with the suspicion a bad one gets for free.
